#770. Jesús López  Steps Down as Head of Universal Music Latin America/Iberian Penninsula, Named Chairman Emeritus of UMG’s Global Talent Services

López led UMG's Latin business for nearly 30 years.

Jesús López, the longtime head of Universal Music’s entire Latin music business and one of the most iconic and influential executives in Latin music, will step down from his longtime position as chairman/CEO of Universal Music Latin America/Iberian Penninsula, Billboard can officially announce.

López will take on a new role as chairman emeritus for Global Talent Services (GTS), the UMG artist management, booking, promotion and services company that he launched in 2007 and which today has offices in eight countries. In his new capacity, he will continue to provide his longtime expertise and knowledge of the Spanish-language music market and its artists. Narcis Rebollo will remain as president/CEO of GTS.

On the label side, López has been working with Sir Lucian Grainge, chairman and CEO of UMG, to put in place a succession plan, “with details to be announced in due course,” according to a Universal release. No further information about a successor was available at press time.

“Jesús is an industry icon who has helped change the course of Latin music on the world stage,” said Grainge in a statement. “Throughout our industry’s evolution he has been a tireless advocate for the creative community, building a team that has advanced the careers of countless superstars. I’m grateful for the care he’s taken to prepare the business for the future and delighted that he’ll help shape the future of GTS, a company born of his own vision for serving artists. I look forward to continuing our work together.”

López added: “As I begin this next chapter within UMG, I’m incredibly proud of what we’ve built together: a company that believes in artists early, stays with them and helps their music travel further than anyone imagined. I look forward to welcoming my successor and supporting our teams as they build on that success. As Chairman of GTS, I will continue pursuing a passion that has guided my entire career: helping artists realize the full scope of their ambitions. I’m grateful to Lucian for his trust and support over so many years, and excited to continue working with him and our teams to create new opportunities for artists.”

López’s transition marks the end of an era for Universal, where he’s held leadership label roles for nearly 30 years.

A native of Spain, he started working at indie labels Movieplay and Hispavox (home at the time to major recording stars like Raphael) before eventually going to Ariola (which later would become BMG) as managing director and garnering his first major international success with Spanish pop group Mecano. BMG eventually appointed him president of its Mexico operations, where he began signing Latin American acts, including a fledgling Gloria Trevi, before moving to Miami and spearheading the international development of Los Del Río and their hit “Macarena,” among other acts. From BMG, López moved to MCA, which would become UMG and where he remained as the head of the company’s Latin division since its onset in the late 1990s.

López’s tenure at Universal has been marked by both artist development and business acumen, including the launch of Machete Records — the first Latin urban label under a major and at one time home to Daddy Yankee and Don Omar — and Surco, a partnership with producer Gustavo Santaolalla to house alternative and rock en español releases, including those by new signee Juanes.

In fact, in a 2015 interview with Billboard, when asked what his greatest accomplishment of all time was, López specifically mentioned his work with rock en español dating back to the late ’80s in Mexico and the launch of Surco: “I took what was in the streets — all these burgeoning bands,” he said at the time. “Rock acts stopped being niche acts and went mainstream, they started to play huge concerts. It’s the most visionary thing I’ve done in my career. I didn’t create anything. It was there. But now it’s a normal part of the musical and cultural Latin landscape.”

However, López’s biggest achievement may have been engineering the global breakthrough of a series of major releases, including Enrique Iglesias‘ “Bailando,” Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee’s landmark “Despacito” and J Balvin and Willy William’s “Mi Gente,” and their ensuing remixes with Justin Bieber (“Despacito”) and Beyoncé (“Mi Gente”).

Most recently, on Nov. 6, López was honored as “Honorary Academician” by the Spanish Academy of Music.

Moving forward, in addition to his work with GTS, he’ll continue to work with producer Julio Reyes Copello’s Art House and Art House Academy in developing new Latin talent, which so far has included Latin Grammy Best New Artist winners Joaquina (2023) and Ela Taubert (2024).

#768. Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon

Far below the ocean's surface, a constant snowfall drifts through the darkness. But unlike the frozen flakes that fall from the sky, this underwater snow consists of tiny clumps of waste, dead organisms, and other debris. Known as marine snow, these particles contain everything from mucus and animal feces to silt and the remains of microscopic plankton.

As this material sinks, it carries enormous quantities of carbon from the upper ocean toward the seafloor. Researchers estimate that marine snow removes more than 10 gigatons of carbon from surface waters each year. Yet only about two gigatons reach depths where that carbon can remain stored for hundreds or even thousands of years.

Why so much carbon fails to make it into the deep ocean has long puzzled scientists. Now, researchers from UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the University of Lincoln have identified a surprisingly important factor: how sticky the marine snow is.

Their findings, published October 8 in the journal Science, show that the viscosity, or thickness and gooeyness, of marine snow influences how quickly bacteria break it apart and how far it can sink. According to the researchers, the stickiest particles can transport more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as particles with a thinner, less viscous consistency.

Marine snow plays an important role in Earth's carbon cycle, the natural movement of carbon among the atmosphere, oceans, land, and living organisms. By transporting carbon into deep water, sinking particles can keep some of it isolated from the atmosphere for centuries or longer.

However, not every particle survives the journey. Bacteria feed on marine snow as it descends, gradually breaking down the material and affecting how much carbon reaches the ocean's depths.

The new research provides the first detailed look at how living bacteria interact with the physical structure of marine snow and, more broadly, mucus itself. These interactions are important well beyond the ocean's carbon cycle. Similar relationships between bacteria and mucus help sustain coral reefs, kelp forests, plant root systems, and the digestive systems of humans and other animals.

Until recently, scientists lacked the technology to observe these interactions at the microscopic scale needed to understand them.

A Four-Year Quest to See Inside Marine Snow

The project began in 2021, when Bryce Inman, then a postdoctoral researcher at Scripps Oceanography, set out to explore what he calls "the muscoscape."

"Observing individual bacteria interacting with the physical structure of mucus had never been possible," said Inman.

Together with colleagues including Farooq Azam, a microbiologist and professor emeritus at Scripps, Inman spent four years trying to overcome that limitation. Multiple attempts were unsuccessful before the team finally developed a working technique in 2025.

Their solution combined 3D confocal microscopy with specially designed fluorescent molecules. Confocal microscopy uses light to capture detailed images at different depths within a sample, allowing researchers to reconstruct its structure in three dimensions. The fluorescent molecules helped make features of the material visible.

For the first time, the scientists could examine the "physical terrain" of individual marine snow particles while watching how living bacteria moved through and interacted with them.

The images revealed a surprisingly intricate microscopic environment, complete with structural differences that affect where bacteria can settle and how easily they can reach the material inside.

Much like snowflakes in the atmosphere, marine snow particles vary considerably. Each contains its own mixture of organic and inorganic materials, creating differences in composition, structure, and viscosity.

The researchers' new imaging approach, described in a companion study published in Nature Communications, revealed that bacteria preferentially colonize areas near a particle's surface where the material is less viscous.

The denser, stickier regions deeper inside are much harder for bacteria to penetrate.

"Bacteria can latch on to less viscous portions of each particle, but cannot reach more viscous regions until they break it down," said Inman. "Think of it like a worm in an apple: the flesh is easy to penetrate, but the core is tough to chew through"

This difference has important consequences for how long marine snow remains intact.

In laboratory experiments, the scientists observed that particles with greater viscosity resisted bacterial degradation and fragmentation for longer periods. Computer simulations further suggested that these stickier particles can descend to greater depths before breaking apart.

Based on these results, the team estimates that highly viscous marine snow can deliver more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as less viscous particles.

The findings help explain why some sinking material transports carbon much farther into the ocean than other particles, even though both begin their journeys near the surface.

"How far marine snow can sink is a surprisingly complicated problem, and we have added another - very gooey - piece to the puzzle," said Inman.

A Discovery With Implications Beyond the Ocean

Although the research focuses on marine snow, its implications extend to many environments where bacteria interact with mucus.

Mucus is often regarded as a relatively simple, slippery substance. But the new imaging technology reveals that it has a complex internal landscape, with microscopic structures that can influence how bacteria behave.

Understanding these physical features could help scientists investigate biological processes in settings ranging from human digestive health to the recovery of damaged coral reefs.

The method also opens opportunities to explore interactions that previously could not be observed directly, providing researchers with a new way to study the microscopic environments inhabited by bacteria.

Mucus, slime, whatever you want to call it, "has a surprising amount of structure," Inman said. "There are bulges, crevasses, all this sort of structure to it that we really had no idea about at a scale smaller than bacteria. This is the first time we're really examining this physical habitat."

The discovery adds an important missing piece to scientists' understanding of how carbon travels through the ocean. It also demonstrates that something as seemingly ordinary as the thickness of underwater slime can have far-reaching consequences for the planet's natural systems.

Additional funding for the research was provided by the Simons Foundation and the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council.

#766. Franco-Moroccan Director Nabil Ayouch on Exploring ‘More Intimacy in My Characters’ With Next Film ‘Run, With No Tears’

For Franco-Moroccan filmmaker Nabil Ayouch, the freedom to tell the stories in which he believes has always mattered more than winning universal approval. Over nearly three decades, he has built a career exploring complex social realities and giving a voice to characters determined to challenge the limits imposed upon their lives. Along the way, he has learned to embrace the possibility that his films won’t always be understood.

“Making films means taking the risk of being misunderstood,” Ayouch tells Variety at the 47th Cairo Intl. Film Festival, where he serves as president of the international competition jury and was honored with the Golden Pyramid Lifetime Achievement Award at the festival’s opening ceremony. “Everyone wants to be loved. But if all I wanted was to be loved, I think I’d do something other than cinema.” Related Stories 'Cher Adores Michael Douglas,' Icon's Rep Says After Douglas Disses Her Oscar Win for 'Moonstruck' 8 Standout Moments From the Governors Awards: Glenn Close Finally Gets Her Oscar, Diane Warren Pitches Olivia Wilde a Christmas Song and More

“It’s more important for me to express myself, to say what I have to say, to try to be understood, to touch souls, than to be loved,” he adds.

His return to Cairo carries particular significance. Nearly three decades ago, Ayouch presented his debut feature, “Mektoub,” at the festival, where it won two awards. Since then, he has returned several times, drawn to a city whose energy he describes as both overwhelming and exhilarating.

But the convictions that first drove Ayouch to make films remain as strong as ever. “The rage that has driven me since I started making cinema is intact, perhaps even stronger today,” he reflects, pointing to the injustices he sees around the world. “Every morning, I wake up full of this energy, this anger, but also full of love and passion for human beings. I want to continue seeing the beauty of this world and telling it through films.”

That tension between anger and hope has its roots in Ayouch’s childhood in Sarcelles, a working-class suburb north of Paris, where he spent his formative years. He credits the teachers and youth workers at a local youth and cultural center with helping him channel difficult experiences into something constructive.

“They taught me how to transform things that hurt me and that rage into a saving energy,” he recalls. “I don’t think I would have become a director” without them.

The experience has shaped not only his filmmaking but also his efforts to support emerging talent. Ayouch has opened seven cultural centers across Morocco, hoping to offer young people opportunities similar to those that changed his own life.

His films, from “Ali Zaoua” and “Casablanca Beats” to “Much Loved” and “Everybody Loves Touda,” have consistently focused on people seeking to take control of their own lives. But Ayouch resists defining his characters solely through their suffering.

“I need to meet someone whose soul attracts me, not simply because they’ve had a difficult life, but because of their desire to escape a cage, to break free from something that confines them,” he says. “I don’t like characters who are victims.”

Ayouch believes his refusal to portray women as powerless was a key reason “Much Loved,” his 2015 drama about sex workers in Marrakech, sparked such controversy in Morocco.

“Things would have been much simpler if the women in the film had been poor women who were beaten from beginning to end,” he says. “It’s because they’re seeking independence, because they’re demanding and want to escape their circumstances, that the film caused so much trouble.”

The controversy surrounding “Much Loved” prompted moments of doubt, but Ayouch insists that provoking outrage has never been his objective.

“I don’t make films to create controversy,” he maintains. “I make films because something outrages me, and I can’t imagine that those films won’t be divisive.”

Ayouch is a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and France’s Académie des Césars. As president of Cairo’s international competition jury, he prefers to enter screenings knowing as little as possible about the filmmakers or their stories.

“I like to be surprised,” he says. “Cinema is an encounter, a shock, a moment of wonder.” He is particularly drawn to films that continue to reveal themselves long after the credits roll.

When it comes to jury deliberations, he favors discussion and consensus over voting, hoping that the jury’s diverse perspectives will help them reach a collective decision rather than one imposed by majority rule.

Despite receiving a lifetime achievement award, Ayouch is hardly ready to call it a day. He jokingly dubbed it a “mid-lifetime achievement award,” making clear that he hopes to have plenty more films ahead of him.

Looking ahead, he is interested in a different approach. “I’d like to explore a little more intimacy in my characters,” he reveals. “To make cinema that’s less political, and to find politics elsewhere, particularly in intimacy.”

That exploration will continue with his next feature, “Run, With No Tears,” which is scheduled to begin shooting in Morocco in early January. The film will star Vimala Pons, who replaces the previously announced Noomi Rapace, alongside Maryam Touzani and Nisrin Erradi, reuniting Ayouch with two actresses from his previous work. The film will be produced via his company Ali n’ Productions.

While he is eager to explore new directions, Ayouch has little interest in revisiting or correcting his earlier work. “If I had to remake the films I’ve made, I’d remake them all, scene by scene, film by film, and change absolutely nothing.”

#765. Number of international students arriving in US plunges — worrying scientists

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dan Garisto is a freelance reporter in Syracuse, New York.

International students earn almost 40% of science and engineering PhDs awarded in the United States.Credit: Bill Pugliano/Getty

The number of international students arriving in the United States in August for the start of the academic year has fallen by 28% since 2024, reaching the lowest level since the depths reached in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Data from the federal National Travel and Tourism Office show that the number of incoming student-visa holders fell from 387,000 in August 2024 to 277,000 in August 2026 (see ‘Students stay away’). The trend has been driven by a decline in the numbers of students from India and China, which dropped by about 50,000 and 23,000, respectively, from 2024 to 2026.

Source: National Travel and Tourism Office (NTTO); Nature analysis.

The number of applications from international students to US PhD programmes has also declined over the past year, falling by 21% from 2025 to 2026, according to a survey of 55 members of the Association of American Universities (AAU), a coalition of research-intensive schools.

These decreases are squeezing already strained university budgets, and researchers worry about the impact on US science. “I can’t imagine a more effective way for the US to cede its dominance in critical scientific fields to China and Europe than by reducing international students,” says Nigel Goldenfeld, a physicist at the University of California, San Diego. In 2024, international students earned 38% of the science and engineering PhDs awarded in the United States.

The great university shake-up: four charts show how global higher education is changing

The great university shake-up: four charts show how global higher education is changing

The administration of US President Donald Trump has introduced several restrictions on visas and international travel since Trump took office in early 2025. Last month, the administration also attempted to place a US$100,000 levy on science and engineering students enrolling in extended Optional Practical Training (OPT), a work programme used by hundreds of thousands of recent graduates and the largest pipeline of scientific talent into the United States. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which issued the proposal, stated that it is meant to “combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect U.S. workers”.

Federal judges have suspended the OPT charge and other efforts that the administration made to curb immigration. But higher-education specialists link these attempts to the large decrease in new overseas students, who, they say, can no longer count a US education as a stable investment. “Uncertainty has become policy, and that has registered in the hearts and minds of students,” says Chris Glass, a higher-education researcher at Boston College in Massachusetts.

The United Kingdom, Canada and Australia have also seen drops in enrolment of international students after placing new limits on these populations. But the US policies are especially restrictive, Glass says.

A spokesperson for the White House did not respond to Nature’s request for comment.

#764. Stronger flu shot linked to nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk

A higher dose of the annual flu vaccine may offer older adults an unexpected benefit: a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease.

In a large study led by researchers at UTHealth Houston, adults ages 65 and older who received a high-dose influenza vaccine were less likely to develop Alzheimer's than those given the standard-dose version. The findings, published in the medical journal Neurology, suggest that the strength of a flu vaccine could matter for more than just protection against influenza.

The discovery grew out of an unexpected conversation between a UTHealth Houston physician and local public health officials. What began as a visit to discuss earlier vaccine research eventually led scientists to investigate whether different flu vaccine doses might be associated with different levels of Alzheimer's risk.

A Surprising Connection Between Flu Vaccines and Alzheimer's

Alzheimer's disease is the leading cause of dementia and an increasingly serious public health concern. In 2025, more than 7 million Americans ages 65 and older were living with the disease, representing approximately 1 in 9 people in that age group. That figure is projected to more than double by 2050.

Researchers have been exploring whether common vaccines might influence the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's. In a 2022 study, a team led by Paul Schulz, MD, found that flu vaccination was associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer's among adults 65 and older.

Schulz is a professor of neurology at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston and director of the Neurocognitive Disorders Center at UTHealth Houston Neurosciences.

Three years after that earlier investigation, Schulz and his colleagues published new research examining a more specific question: Could receiving a stronger flu vaccine be associated with an even greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk?

The idea came from public health officials who had learned about the team's previous findings and invited Schulz to discuss them.

"The public health department had seen our vaccine research and asked if I could come down to talk to them about it," said Schulz, who is the senior author of the study and the Rick McCord Professor in Neurology and Umphrey Family Professor in Neurodegenerative Diseases at McGovern Medical School. "We went through the findings, and they asked if there was a difference with different dosages; I was confused."

Why Older Adults Receive Stronger Flu Shots

As people grow older, their immune systems gradually become less effective at recognizing and fighting infections. This age-related decline can make influenza particularly dangerous for seniors.

To help address that vulnerability, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends high-dose influenza vaccines as a preferred option for adults ages 65 and older. These vaccines contain four times as much influenza antigen as standard-dose shots. Antigens are the components of a vaccine that stimulate the immune system to recognize and defend against a virus.

The higher dose is designed to produce a stronger immune response in older adults, whose immune systems may respond less effectively to conventional vaccines.

Schulz had not previously realized that this stronger formulation was available.

"I was stunned that, as a physician, I didn't know a higher dose was offered," Schulz said.

Annual flu vaccination is recommended broadly, but preventing influenza is especially important for people with Alzheimer's disease. Flu infections and their complications can pose serious health risks for individuals already coping with cognitive impairment.

Before 2022, the CDC did not express a preference for one type of injectable influenza vaccine over another for people ages 65 and older. Instead, the guidance emphasized receiving a flu shot every year, regardless of the specific formulation.

Previous research from UTHealth Houston had already linked inactivated influenza vaccines, which use viruses that cannot cause influenza infection, to a 40% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. However, researchers had not yet determined whether a higher vaccine dose might be associated with additional benefits.

Another practical issue made the question particularly relevant. As the population of older Americans continues to grow, demand for high-dose flu vaccines sometimes exceeds the available supply. Consequently, some seniors receive standard-dose vaccines instead.

This variation gave researchers an opportunity to compare Alzheimer's outcomes among older adults who had received different formulations.

"So we started looking, and sure enough, we were able to put together thousands and thousands of people over the age of 65 who got the high- or low-dose vaccine. They're more at risk for Alzheimer's than anybody else, of course, because it's age-related and we could look at high-dose versus low-dose and see if there was a difference," Schulz said.

Nearly 200,000 Adults Reveal a Significant Difference

To investigate the potential connection, the research team analyzed data from nearly 200,000 men and women ages 65 and older.

The results showed that people who received high-dose influenza vaccines had a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease than those who received the standard-dose formulation.

The researchers reported that standard-dose influenza vaccination was associated with a 40% reduction in Alzheimer's risk, while high-dose vaccination was linked to a reduction of nearly 55%.

The association was particularly pronounced among women, who appeared to experience a greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk with the stronger vaccine.

These findings add to growing evidence of a possible relationship between influenza vaccination and brain health. They also raise important questions about whether the immune response triggered by vaccination might influence biological processes involved in Alzheimer's disease.

However, the findings demonstrate an association rather than establishing cause and effect. Additional research is needed to determine whether high-dose flu vaccination directly reduces the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's and to understand the mechanisms that might explain the connection.

What the Findings Could Mean for Alzheimer's Prevention

With Alzheimer's affecting millions of Americans and the number of cases expected to rise sharply in the coming decades, researchers are searching for practical ways to reduce risk.

The possibility that an existing vaccine could have benefits extending beyond influenza prevention is particularly intriguing. Unlike an entirely new treatment, flu vaccination is already widely used, and higher-dose formulations are specifically designed for older adults.

The new findings suggest that vaccine dosage could be an important consideration in future studies exploring the relationship between the immune system and Alzheimer's disease.

For now, the research provides another reason to investigate the potential benefits of influenza vaccination while emphasizing the need for further studies before drawing conclusions about Alzheimer's prevention.

Avram Samuel Bukhbinder, MD, a graduate of McGovern Medical School who is currently a clinical fellow in neurology at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard University, served as a corresponding author of the study.

Schulz is also a faculty member of The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center UTHealth Houston Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences.

Other contributors from McGovern Medical School included Elizabeth He, visiting scholar in the Department of Neurology; Kristofer Harris, MPH, research coordinator in the Department of Neurology; Mya Rodriguez, graduate research assistant in the Department of Neurology; Kamal Phelps, MD, an alumnus of the Department of Neurology; Jenna Thomas; Gabriela Cruz, MD, resident in the Department of Neurology; and Lauren Jhin.

Researchers from the McWilliams School of Biomedical Informatics at UTHealth Houston also participated. They included Xiaoqian Jiang, PhD, associate vice president for medical AI, chair of the Department of Health Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, and Christopher Sarofim Family Professor in Biomedical Informatics and Bioengineering; Yejin Kim, PhD, assistant professor in the Department of Health Data Science and Artificial Intelligence; Luyao Chen, researcher; and Yaobin Ling, PhD, postdoctoral research fellow.

#763. Grammys Snubs and Surprises: Harry Styles Shut Out, Raye’s Huge Year and Noah Kahan Only Gets One Nomination

The 2027 Grammy nominations have arrived, with some notable breakthroughs and reigning hot streaks from artists including Raye, Rosalía, Phoebe Bridgers, Miranda Lambert, the Olivias (Dean and Rodrigo), Bruno Mars and many more.

As with every year, there are plenty of surprises and just as many snubs among the nominees. Raye and Rosalía were among the artists who had the most unexpected success stories in the top categories, as were some best new artist nominees including Remi Wolf, Angine de Poitrine and the Womack Sisters. Women dominated across numerous categories, while artists like Ariana Grande and Stella Lefty had surprisingly lower-than-expected showings. Variety ticks down the nominees list to break down what was expected — and what wasn’t. Related Stories AFM Dealmakers, Talent Agents and Hollywood Stars Left Stranded by Nationwide Flight Stoppage 8 Standout Moments From the Governors Awards: Glenn Close Finally Gets Her Oscar, Diane Warren Pitches Olivia Wilde a Christmas Song and More

SNUB: Harry Styles shut out entirely. Perhaps the artist with one of the biggest years is also one of the biggest snubs among the 2027 Grammy nominees. Styles had been on a red-hot run amid the release of his fourth studio album “Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally.” He announced the record in January and followed with its lead single “Aperture,” leading into the March release of the project. He then spent the bulk of the year on the road as part of his “Together, Together” world tour that brought him to cities including Amsterdam, London, Mexico City, São Paulo and New York City, where he staged a historic 30-night residency at the famed Madison Square Garden through the end of October. However, the album itself met a polarized reaction, even from hardcore fans.

Among the categories where Styles submitted “KATTDO” were album of the year, best pop vocal album, best engineered album and best album cover. He submitted “Aperture” for record of the year, song of the year, best pop solo performance and best music video; “Coming Up Roses” for best arrangement, instruments, and vocals; and “One Night Only Manchester” for best music film. It’s perplexing that the Recording Academy denied every submission, particularly considering that he has been a Grammy darling for years with nine nominations and three wins, including album of the year for “Harry’s House” in 2023.

SURPRISE: Best new artist category is an unpredictable mixed bag. No one should be surprised by many of these nominees — Ella Langley, Sienna Spiro, Don Toliver, Geese and Slayyyter were largely predicted to secure spots among the class of 2027 — yet it’s the remaining artists that may have some heads scratching for casual music fans, although all certainly have passionate fan bases. Canadian sibling duo Angine de Poitrine has built a very dedicated following that is equally mesmerized by their hypnotic strain of math rock as they are by their black-and-white polka dot costumes. The Womack Sisters, meanwhile, made waves among retro R&B fans with their self-titled debut album that released in August (and yes, they come from a formidable legacy: daughters of singers Cecil and Linda Womack, and nieces of the legendary Bobby). And Remi Wolf, who has been an indie-pop darling since she started putting out music in 2019, is something of a curveball, considering that she released her latest album “Mud” outside of the Grammy submission window and, like many nominees in years past (and some others this year), is far from a new artist.

It’s worth noting the slate of artists who were included in predictions lists from various publications and industry spectators that didn’t make the cut. Malcolm Todd, who had a huge year with his June album “Do That Again,” was left off the ballot, as was his sister Audrey Hobert, whose excellent debut “Who’s the Clown?” was released last year. Sam Fender, Role Model, Stella Lefty, Miles Caton and Bella Kay were also excluded from the category after making noise during the eligibility period.

SURPRISE: Raye leads with the most nominations…which is not entirely shocking, given the consistent goodwill towards Raye and critical praise for her sophomore album “This Music May Contain Hope,” which was released independently in March. The singer-songwriter, who was recently named Variety‘s 2026 Hitmaker of the Year, leads overall nominations with a staggering 11 nods, trailed by Rosalía with nine and Ella Langley, Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo and Phoebe Bridgers with seven. Raye is nominated in all three eligible categories of the Big Four, including album of the year, plus song and record of the year for “Where Is My Husband!” (She was already nominated for best new artist in 2025.) She’s also up for best pop solo performance for “Husband” and best pop duo/group performance for “Click Clack Symphony” featuring Hans Zimmer; best pop vocal album; best dance pop recording for “Life Boat”; best traditional pop vocal performance for “I Hate the Way I Look Today”; best music video for “Click Clack Symphony”; and best arrangement, instruments and vocals for “Click Clack Symphony.”

The only category where she’s nominated that may leave some Grammy scholars puzzled is her inclusion in songwriter of the year (non-classical), where she’s up against Amy Allen, Edgar Barrera, Theron Thomas and Joybeth Taylor — which is confusing because the honor was intended to recognize songwriters whose work was largely recorded by others. Among her credits are five of her own songs, plus four others where she has a songwriting credit but is not the main artist (Amma’s “God Be My Witness”; Halle and GloRilla’s “Know About Me”; Sonny Fodera and Libianca’s “Let Me Be in Your Arms”; and Say Now’s “Supermarket”). According to Academy rules, songwriters must submit a minimum of four songs in which they’re credited as a songwriter or co-writer, and songs where the songwriter was credited as a Primary or Featured Artist or Producer do not qualify to meet the minimum threshold. Translated to layman’s terms, Raye qualifies in this category because she met the threshold with credits as a songwriter for other artists’ songs.

SNUB: Noah Kahan receives only one nomination. It seemed as though the singer-songwriter may have been steeling himself — and prepping his fans — for Grammy disappointment on Sunday after he tweeted, “Whatever happens tomorrow I love you all and I have done everything I’ve ever needed to do in my career because of YOUR support. You guys are all I care about.” The reality may be even more sobering, considering that Kahan had a gargantuan year and was predicted to secure nominations in the top and genre categories. Instead, he only picks up a single nomination in best contemporary folk album for “The Great Divide: The Last of the Bugs,” the expanded edition of his fourth album that initially dropped in April. This really did seem to be his shot at Grammy glory, given he’s only gotten two nods before (best new artist in 2024 and best country duo/group performance in 2025), but it looks like it’s better luck next year for one Mr. Kahan.

SURPRISE-ISH: Major female dominance in top categories. Really not much of a surprise, considering the large swath of female artists who gave the industry a run for its money over the past year. Six out of eight record of the year nominees are songs by women (the seventh, Tame Impala’s “Dracula,” features Jennie). Bruno Mars is the only man to be nominated for album of the year with “The Romantic,” up against Phoebe Bridgers, Raye, Olivia Rodrigo, Olivia Dean, Rosalía, Ella Langley and Taylor Swift. Seven out of eight of the song of the year nominees are by women (Mars, again, offers a speck of diversity). And girl power isn’t just limited to the biggest categories: all of the nominees in best dance pop recording, best R&B solo performance, best traditional pop vocal performance and best contemporary country album are by women.

SNUB: Ariana Grande picks up fewer than expected. Admittedly, Grande hasn’t historically been a heavily nominated artist. The most nods she received in one year was in 2020, when she picked up five. But given how well her latest album “Petal” performed, as did its lead single “Hate That I Made You Love Me,” Grande was expected to have a stronger showing for the 2027 awards. Next year, she’ll be competing in four categories: song of the year for “Hate That I Made You Love Me,” best pop vocal album for “Petal,” best traditional pop vocal performance for “For Good” with Cynthia Erivo and best music video for “Hate That I Made You Love Me.” (“Petal” is up for a fifth award, in best immersive audio album, though Grande herself is not nominated.) This is certainly a snub for Grande who, despite picking up some substantial nods, was left out of album of the year, record of the year and all the other genre categories she submitted — surprising, considering that artists like Taylor Swift, Olivia Rodrigo and Rosalía got nominated in all three major categories where they were eligible.

SURPRISE: Speaking of, Rosalía’s “Berghain,” hardly a traditional mainstream single, gets nods for record and song of the year. You’d be hard-pressed to find anyone who doesn’t consider Rosalía’s “Lux” to be a pop masterpiece, yet many of those same folks would probably agree that “Berghain” is far from what you’d consider a “mainstream” single. The track, featuring Björk and Yves Tumor, is like a 21st-century cantata, replete with vamping strings and ominous choral chants. Even with a cursory glance at the song and record of the year nominees, “Berghain” sticks out like a sore thumb, showing that genuine musicians are voting and appreciate the artistry of Rosalía’s production and songwriting.

SNUB: Stella Lefty’s “Boston,” one of the biggest singles of the year, gets ignored. Following in Alex Warren’s “Ordinary” footsteps from earlier this year, Stella Lefty’s “Boston” may be one of the biggest songs of 2026, but that is of little concern to voting members. The track has been a commercial juggernaut, reaching No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100, yet has been consistently dogged by accusations of plagiarism, as fans have noted its striking similarities to Kahan’s “Stick Season.” Academy members fell in line with the critical consensus, it seems… And while Warren may have ended up with at least one nomination for best new artist, Lefty comes up empty-handed for next year.

#761. First Lady Melania Trump to Participate in Fox News’ Annual Christmas Tree Lighting

The relationship between Fox News and President Donald Trump has been strained in recent months, but it clearly endures.

The Fox News All-American Christmas Tree will stand at 50 feet tall, and will be decorated with 18,000 ornaments and 340,000 warm white, true white and red lights. The tree is made by holiday lighting and display company American Christmas based in Mt. Vernon, N.Y., and will have a six-foot-tall dove topper with 4,800 embedded lights.

Mrs. Trump’s appearance on Fox News comes after her husband, President Donald Trump, appeared to place some of the blame for Republicans being largely defeated by Democrats in the nation’s recent midterm elections on the network itself. “FoxNews bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition, and worse,” Trump said via a post on Truth Social on the night of the elections. In other posts, President Trump attacked Fox News’ polls, which are widely regarded in the news sector, and criticized a decision to feature Jessica Tarlov, a Democrat who is also a co-host on “The Five.” Tarlov is not listed as appearing on the Christmas special.

Even so, Trump did call in to speak with Fox News anchors Bret Baier and Martha MacCallum on Election Night.

The Christmas special has become a regular part of the Fox News programming calendar, much like CNN’s annual telecast of New Year’s Eve festivities in Times Square is a bedrock element of its end-of-year schedule. CNN has recently tried to expand its hosting duo for that night, Anderson Cooper and Andy Cohen, to other holidays, such as the Fourth of July.

Guests in the past at the Fox News Christmas Tree Lighting have included Chris Tomlin and Gavin DeGraw.

Steve Doocy and Carley Shimkus will also participate in the evening. Doocy, a longtime co-host of “Fox & Friends,” will serve as “Christmas correspondent” for the evening, while Shimkus, a co-host of the early-morning “Fox & Friends First,” will lead social content. Both will offer viewers inside looks at Fox News Media studios along with exclusive interviews with special guests. Lauren Green, Fox News Channel’s chief religion correspondent, will introduce Reverend Franklin Graham and actor Jonathan Roumie as they offer a blessing to the audience.

Fox News Media has partnered with Armed Services YMCA, an organization dedicated to assisting junior enlisted service members and their families as they navigate deployments, relocations, and the everyday sacrifices of military life. FOX News Media employees helped pack stockings filled with gifts for deployed service members and wrote personalized welcome-home cards for troops returning for the holidays.

#760. Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease

Tick-borne illnesses are becoming increasingly common across the United States, and Lyme disease remains the most frequently reported. Nearly 500,000 Americans are diagnosed each year. The infection is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, which typically reaches humans through the bite of an infected blacklegged tick. Antibiotics can treat Lyme disease, but without treatment, the infection may affect the joints, heart, and nervous system. Some patients also experience symptoms that persist over time.

Now, one of the longest-running studies of Lyme disease ecology is challenging several assumptions about what makes the disease more likely to spread. For more than 35 years, scientists at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in Millbrook, New York, have tracked the complicated relationships among ticks, mice, oak trees, predators, and weather. Their research has uncovered unexpected patterns that could help predict when people face greater exposure to infected ticks.

A new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences brings together nine of the project's most surprising discoveries. The findings show how decades of observations can reveal connections that shorter studies might miss.

"On balance, these surprises have enriched our knowledge of this system, helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk," said lead author Richard Ostfeld, a disease ecologist at the Cary Institute who leads the research program alongside Shannon LaDeau.

According to Ostfeld, the extensive data collected over the years have been essential for separating meaningful ecological patterns from coincidences and statistical fluctuations.

"Studies of this depth and length are incredibly rare," said LaDeau. "This research has followed an ecological community -- including oak trees, mammals, and microorganisms -- examining how interactions like predation, parasitism, and competition shape the system over time. The evolution of understanding summarized in this paper is something you simply cannot get without such a long-term and system-focused study."

Deer May Play a Smaller Role in Lyme Disease Risk Than Expected

When Lyme disease first gained recognition in the United States during the 1980s, white-tailed deer were considered a likely driver of rising tick populations. Hunters frequently encountered deer carrying numerous adult ticks, suggesting that areas with more deer might also produce more ticks.

The reasoning seemed straightforward. Although deer cannot pass the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks, they provide blood meals for adult female ticks. Scientists suspected that larger deer populations would allow more female ticks to reproduce, eventually increasing the number of young ticks capable of spreading the infection.

But decades of monitoring have produced a different picture. On the Cary Institute's 2,000-acre forested research property in Dutchess County, New York, researchers found no statistically significant connection between deer numbers and the abundance of nymphal ticks. Nymphs are immature ticks responsible for much of the Lyme disease transmission to humans.

"We had detected a weak positive relationship between deer and subsequent nymph abundance over short subsets of the data," said Ostfeld, "but the whole data set in its entirety shows no such thing."

Mice Are a Much Stronger Predictor of Tick Surges

While deer populations failed to predict the abundance of nymphal ticks, mouse populations showed a much clearer relationship.

Years with especially large mouse populations were followed by approximately 40% more nymphal ticks the next year. White-footed mice are particularly important because they provide excellent blood meals for tick larvae and are highly effective at transmitting Borrelia burgdorferi to those feeding on them.

Once infected as larvae, ticks can retain the bacteria as they develop into nymphs. When these nymphs take another blood meal, they can pass the infection to humans.

The findings suggest that tracking mouse populations could provide a valuable early warning of unusually high tick numbers.

How Acorns Can Predict Tick Populations Two Years Ahead

One of the most unexpected discoveries involves something that might seem entirely unrelated to Lyme disease: acorns.

Oak trees periodically produce exceptionally large crops of acorns in synchronized events known as acorn masting. These unusually productive years provide an abundance of food for forest rodents, allowing mouse populations to expand during the following year.

That increase in mice then supports larger numbers of young ticks. As a result, the researchers found that a particularly heavy acorn crop can reliably predict an increase in nymphal ticks two years later.

The relationship reveals a remarkable sequence of events in which the reproductive cycle of forest trees helps determine future tick abundance. It also offers researchers another potential tool for anticipating periods of greater Lyme disease exposure.

Why More Mice Don't Always Mean More Infected Ticks

Although mouse abundance helps predict how many nymphal ticks will appear, the researchers discovered that it does not consistently predict what percentage of those ticks will carry Lyme disease bacteria.

Initially, scientists expected both measures to rise together. Because mice are efficient transmitters of B. burgdorferi, an increase in mice seemed likely to produce not only more ticks but also a greater proportion of infected ticks.

Early observations appeared to support that idea. However, as additional years of data accumulated, the apparent relationship gradually disappeared.

"It kept me up at night," said Ostfeld, "because it meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong."

The explanation appears to involve the other animals that share the forest with mice. Skunks, squirrels, and opossums also serve as hosts for feeding ticks, but most are much less effective at passing the Lyme disease bacterium to them.

When these animals are abundant, more larval ticks may feed on hosts that are unlikely to infect them. This can reduce the percentage of nymphal ticks carrying the bacteria, even when mouse populations are high.

"So the infection prevalence in the nymphs really depends on how all the larval tick meals are distributed across all the hosts," explained Ostfeld. "It would have been convenient if one host predicted that for us, but that has not been the case."

This finding highlights an important distinction between the total number of ticks in an environment and the proportion carrying the pathogen. Predicting the risk of infection requires understanding the broader community of animals that ticks feed on, not simply counting mice.

Extreme Heat and Cold May Not Kill Ticks in the Wild

Weather has also produced some unexpected results.

Earlier laboratory experiments suggested that exposure to intense heat or severe cold could kill blacklegged ticks. Yet observations in natural habitats revealed that ticks are surprisingly capable of surviving these conditions.

Researchers believe ticks protect themselves from temperature extremes by retreating into deeper soil layers or hiding beneath fallen leaves, where conditions are less severe than at the surface.

However, the long-term data also revealed a more complicated relationship with temperature. Years that are warmer overall tend to be followed by fewer nymphal ticks than usual, despite the ability of individual ticks to withstand short periods of extreme heat.

At the same time, warmer conditions generally favor mouse populations, which can lead to more ticks. These opposing effects make it difficult to predict how changing temperatures will ultimately influence Lyme disease risk.

What 35 Years of Research Mean for Lyme Disease Prevention

Taken together, the discoveries show that Lyme disease risk depends on a network of ecological interactions that is complicated but not entirely unpredictable.

Mouse abundance, for example, provides a stronger indicator of future nymphal tick numbers than deer abundance at the study site. Similarly, unusually harsh winters may not reduce tick populations as dramatically as previously expected.

By understanding these patterns, public health officials may be better equipped to anticipate periods of increased tick exposure and develop more effective prevention strategies.

Still, important questions remain, particularly about how climate change will affect ticks, the animals they feed on, and the oak trees that influence rodent populations.

"You would expect that a warming climate, which makes life better for the mice, would eventually make life better for the ticks, but we have not seen that so far," said Ostfeld. "We need to know what to expect from the different manifestations of climate change, which are sometimes warmer and drier, and sometimes warmer and wetter. The time of year when it's very warm also matters to ticks, oaks, and acorn production."

The research site in Dutchess County has undergone significant environmental changes since monitoring began in 1991. Climate shifts, changes to the surrounding landscape, and the arrival of invasive species have all altered the conditions in which the forest's plants and animals live.

Researchers intend to continue following these changes to determine how ticks and their hosts respond over time. Their work could provide increasingly valuable insights into how future environmental changes will influence human exposure to Lyme disease and other infections carried by ticks.

Materials provided by Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#759. ‘Ramayana: Rise of a Legend’ Review: Indian Mythological Blockbuster Is an Eye-Popper, but Skip the English Edit

Already a global hit, the first part of Nitesh Tiwari's megabudget adaptation of the Hindu epic poem alternates cardboard drama with exhilarating spectacle — but either way, it's better without the AI lipsyncing.

There are currently two versions of “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” screening in most English-language markets: the 208-minute Hindi-language original version, replete with a wealth of musical numbers complementing its bombastic action, and a 166-minute edit shorn of songs, with its dialogue “dubbed” into English via AI lipsyncing technology. My first encounter with Nitesh Tiwari‘s blockbuster epic was a press screening of the latter cut, and I rather wish it hadn’t been. I left with the sense of having witnessed only a fraction of an inevitable popular phenomenon — a return to the bad old days when it was believed that foreign genre fare had to meet Anglophone audiences at precisely their level and lingo, only this time translated in more eerily state-of-the-art fashion. Related Stories Hollywood Still Faces Weekend Disruptions After FAA Lifts Flight Ground Stop AFM Dealmakers, Talent Agents and Hollywood Stars Left Stranded by Nationwide Flight Stoppage

Catching up with the full version, however, with its uncompromised breadth and comfortingly analog English subtitles, the film comes into its own. It might be a stretch to say that “Ramayana” loses its soul in translation: Tiwari’s adaptation of the Sanskrit epic poem of the same title remains a fairly synthetic spectacle in any language, awash with gaudy CGI and stiff scripting either way. But it feels most expressive in its most sprawling form, not least because the film’s musical numbers account for many of its most vivid peaks. (Who goes to a Bollywood extravaganza and doesn’t want the songs? You may as well cut the car chases from a “Fast & Furious” movie.)

You can partially see the reasoning, since minus most of the musical element (preserved, in the shorter version, in just a few interstitial montages that feature no onscreen singing), the Hollywood template for “Ramayana” is even more apparent. Though the film, with its super-sized treatment of an ancient narrative, may seem like the Indian film industry’s answer to “The Odyssey,” the execution is more Marvel-adjacent: Effectively, the film refashions its venerable source text — the life story of the Hindu deity Rama, shot through with philosophical and moral teachings — as a kind of superhero origin story, short on spiritual reflection and long on derring-do. And as all such movies now must do, it tells only part of the story, ending on a near-literal cliffhanger before a title card promises Part Two at Diwali 2028.

It’s a slightly annoying cutoff, but not an exasperating one: Even at three-plus hours, the film doesn’t get us so emotionally invested in the journey of its somewhat colorless hero that we leave feeling we can’t possibly wait two years to see how the saga turns out. The chief rewards of “Ramayana” are ones of sheer sensory abundance, from the rampaging orchestrations of the score — a pounding East-meets-West collaboration between Oscar winners A.R. Rahman and Hans Zimmer — to the iridescent kaleidoscope formations of the production and costume design.

In the most expensive production in Indian film history, you can’t complain that the money isn’t on the screen: It may indeed be among the most physically gilded films ever made. No scene is bedecked with one twirling, petal-tossing extra when a couple dozen will do; assorted flying hybrid creatures glide through elaborate battle scenes as little more than show-offy window-dressing. (Visual effects, courtesy of the U.K.-Indian studio DNEG, range from the robustly impressive to the chintzy.)

The story amid all the setpieces is bitty but straightforward enough: It darts heedlessly across chronological chasms, though in terms of what it covers from the text, it amounts to little more than throat-clearing. An opening battle sequence lays out the backstory of longtime conflict between two rival classes of divine being, the Asuras and the Devas. Defeated in the latest round of war, the Asuras appoint young Ravana (Yash, also one of the film’s producers) as their leader, though not before years of lone meditation, after which he’s granted invincible powers by the creator Brahma, and reclaims the kingdom of Lanka from the Devas. In retaliation, the god Vishnu selects the Devas prince Rama (eventually played as an adult by Ranbir Kapoor) as his human-born avatar.

All of which is to say “Ramayana” hurtles through an entire act before its eponymous hero is even identified as such. A showdown between good Rama and evil Ravana is clearly on the cards, or in the stars, but there’s a whole lot more story to get through before then: Rama’s marriage to strong-willed princess Sita (Sai Pallavi); the loss, through corrupt means, of his promised throne to brother Bharata (Adinath Kothare); and his long-term exile to the wilderness, accompanied by Sita and loyal half-brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey), who’s unluckily, and unfunnily, handed the portfolio of wisecracking sidekick.

The script, while chock full of incident, isn’t terribly lively; the characters are hollow vessels of virtue, or lack thereof, affording none of the actors much scope for charm or dynamism. Dialogue is not a strength of the film in any language, though the uncanny-valley lipsyncing in the English version rather exacerbates its lifelessness — one more reason to seek out the longer edit. And yet, treated as a pageant rather than a drama, “Ramayana” has undeniable heft and splendor; even when its craft contributions verge on the lurid or the ersatz, the more-is-more excess of it bludgeons you into a manner of awe. It’s a brawny reminder that blockbuster assembly is a fully global industry these days; Tiwari may borrow a lot from Hollywood, but it’s not hard to see Hollywood borrowing some back.

#758. Mysterious gas leaks suggest Mars may still be volcanically alive

Mars may not be as geologically inactive as it appears. New evidence from mysterious gas emissions near an enormous Martian volcano suggests that heat and volcanic processes could still be present deep beneath the planet's surface.

Researchers have identified unusual concentrations of hydrogen chloride gas above fractures in the Alba Mons volcanic region. The findings suggest that gases from the planet's interior may be escaping through cracks in the surface, potentially revealing volcanic activity that has remained hidden until now.

An international team led by Alexander Trokhimovskiy believes the gas could originate from hot magma underground. If confirmed, this would indicate that Mars still has dormant volcanic systems capable of releasing gases to the surface.

The European Space Agency's ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) first detected hydrogen chloride in the Martian atmosphere in findings reported in 2021. On Earth, hydrogen chloride is frequently released through openings connected to magma, raising the possibility that similar processes could be occurring on Mars.

"Our findings suggest that Mars has retained enough internal heat to support volcanic activity until recently, and possibly still does," says Daniel Mège, Professor at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences and co-lead author of the study published in Science Advances.

Mysterious Gas Emissions Defy Mars' Seasonal Pattern

The researchers noticed something unusual during early summer in the Martian northern hemisphere. Hydrogen chloride concentrations were unexpectedly elevated in a particular region, even though the gas normally becomes scarce at that time of year.

Hydrogen chloride levels on Mars generally follow a seasonal cycle. They typically peak during northern winter before declining to very low levels in summer. Scientists believe much of this behavior is associated with the planet's dust and water cycles.

However, the observations revealed a striking exception. Elevated hydrogen chloride repeatedly appeared in early summer over volcanic fractures on the slopes of Alba Mons. The unusual timing and consistent location suggested that something beyond ordinary atmospheric chemistry might be responsible.

Mars is home to the largest volcanoes in the Solar System, but scientists still do not know whether volcanic processes remain active beneath their surfaces.

Images taken from orbit indicate that some Martian volcanoes experienced eruptions within the past few million years. Instruments on the surface have also recorded marsquakes, demonstrating that the planet continues to experience seismic activity.

Together, these observations suggest that Mars may retain some of its geological energy. However, scientists have never directly observed a new volcanic eruption or fresh lava flow on the planet, leaving the question of present-day volcanism unresolved.

Fresh Cracks Reveal Clues to Hidden Volcanic Heat

To investigate the unusual gas concentrations, the research team combined atmospheric measurements with detailed observations of the Martian surface.

The Atmospheric Chemistry Suite aboard TGO uses infrared spectrometers to identify gases in the atmosphere. These instruments detected hydrogen chloride concentrated in a relatively small area shortly after the disappearance of winter frost.

Researchers then examined the same region using the orbiter's CaSSIS camera. The images revealed narrow fractures that appeared relatively fresh, with some extending hundreds of meters across the surface. Unusual changes in surface color were also visible around the cracks.

"The Trace Gas Orbiter was able to find the smoking gun. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack. It's truly amazing that it spotted a handful of molecules from a perhaps intermittent source, whilst moving continuously along its orbit to monitor the whole Martian atmosphere," explains Daniel.

One possible explanation is that gases originating from magma deep underground travel upward through these fractures. On Earth, comparable volcanic openings are known as fumaroles.

The researchers propose that extremely cold Martian winters, when temperatures can fall to -120°C, allow ice to seal the fractures and temporarily prevent gases from escaping. As temperatures rise in early summer, the ice sublimates, changing directly into vapor and potentially opening pathways for underground gases to reach the atmosphere.

The discoloration observed around the fractures could also be significant. It may result from minerals or other substances deposited by escaping gases, similar to the deposits commonly found around fumaroles (volcanic gas vents) on Earth.

Although the connection between the gas emissions and volcanic fractures appeared promising, the researchers needed to rule out other explanations.

"Looking at the spatial distribution of the seeping, it became instantly obvious to me that there was something volcanic behind it, but it had to be demonstrated," concedes Daniel.

The team carefully evaluated the chemical reactions that could produce hydrogen chloride in the Martian atmosphere, including processes unrelated to volcanism.

"A huge part of the work consisted of examining all the possible chemical processes going on in the Martian atmosphere. We needed to be rigorous, critical and creative to explain the presence of hydrogen chloride. The data were complex, but also excellent brain food," adds Daniel.

After examining the atmospheric and geological evidence together, the researchers proposed that the gas could be escaping from a dormant magma chamber beneath Alba Mons. Such a chamber would form part of an underground volcanic system that could continue releasing gases even without producing visible eruptions.

Hidden Volcanic Activity Could Help Mars Support Life

The implications may extend beyond understanding the planet's geological history. Volcanic gases could also provide clues about how Mars evolved and whether it ever supported environments suitable for life.

In the distant past, gases released from magma, including hydrogen chloride, may have helped create a denser atmosphere and warmer conditions. Those conditions could have allowed liquid water to remain across large portions of the Martian surface.

Volcanic activity might also create habitable environments underground. If rising magma or lava comes into contact with groundwater, the interaction can produce warm hydrothermal systems. Such environments could provide both chemical energy and protection from the harsh conditions on the surface.

"Looking for Martian life in the seeping fissures of the Alba Mons region would make a lot of sense. If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface," ponders Daniel.

Although the findings do not establish that Mars is currently erupting or that life exists beneath its surface, they offer an intriguing new reason to investigate the volcanic fractures around Alba Mons.

"These findings may prove to be TGO's greatest success yet," highlights Colin Wilson, ESA's project scientist for the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter.

#756. Where's the growth? Legacy automakers face a tougher 2027 as costs rise, market tightens

DETROIT — There's a growing concern that the global automotive industry may be stuck in neutral, if not reverse, heading into 2027.

The auto industry — from the companies to their customers — has been surprisingly resilient this decade, but there are fears that rising costs, weaker vehicle pricing and a more challenging market could threaten profits and growth going forward.

Automakers also face pressure outside the U.S. from an onslaught of Chinese carmakers, a thinner new-product pipeline after retreating from some all-electric plans, and company- and region-specific challenges.

"With investor focus increasingly shifting to 2027, the setup appears challenging," Barclays analyst Dan Levy said in an investor note last month. "Rising inflation, continued China pressure, affordability concerns in the U.S., and a flat global production outlook suggest another year of limited earnings growth."

Several Wall Street analysts have said automakers will need continued pricing strength and additional cost savings to offset inflation, higher investment spending and a potentially weaker economy just to maintain their current levels.

"It's a little bit more optimistic in the U.S. and then very pessimistic in Europe," RBC Capital Markets analyst Tom Narayan told CNBC. "As a whole, there's some negativity on '27."

Automakers from the U.S. to Europe to Asia have been facing a growing list of headwinds.

For U.S.-based legacy automakers, Ford Motor said it expects next year's results to be in line with 2026, while General Motors grew more cautious about its ability to continue growing earnings as much as it had previously expected.

"We continue to believe that 2027 will be another strong year and better than 2026, assuming customer demand remains strong, and commodity, logistics and other recent cost pressures moderate," GM CEO Mary Barra told investors Oct. 20.

GM CFO Paul Jacobson said that while it's too early to officially forecast, the company is facing additional inflationary costs that could lead to another $2 billion headwind in 2027, like it expects this year. He specifically cited costs of commodity inflation, logistics and DRAM, or dynamic random-access memory chips as challenges.

Those chips are critical components in modern vehicles and are used for everything from temporary data storage and real-time processing from infotainment systems to safety-critical systems.

GM and others have been able to offset outside pressures through cost cuts, operational efficiencies and resilient consumer demand for higher-margin vehicles. However, there's a limit to what companies can do.

"There's only so much pricing you can push to consumers," Narayan said. "They're already at pretty high pricing."

European automakers including Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz and BMW in recent weeks reduced their 2026 earnings forecasts in response to U.S. tariffs, the growth of Chinese automakers and rising costs.

Most recently, BMW this week said accelerated restructuring measures would reduce its automotive pretax earnings margin this year by 2.5 percentage points. The company said the restructuring should support "positive effects" into 2027 and a 3% to 5% pretax profit margin for 2028. That compares with a 5.3% automotive margin last year and 3.4% during the third quarter.

Chrysler parent Stellantis, which has large operations in Europe and the U.S., is facing its own challenges, as it's in the midst of a restructuring that aims for a low-single-digit adjusted operating margin this year. It has maintained a 2026 guidance that includes a mid-single-digit percentage increase in net revenue and a low-single-digit adjusted operating margin.

In Asia, South Korean automaker Hyundai Motor, which has experienced notable growth in recent years, also cut key metrics when it reported earnings late last month. The company lowered its 2026 wholesales target to 4 million vehicles, down from 4.16 million, and cut its operating-margin target to between 5.5% and 6.5%, down from a previous goal of 6.3% to 7.3%.

Toyota Motor is an outlier for its most recent quarter and outlook, as the world's largest automaker increased its full-year operating income forecast by 500 billion Japanese yen (about $3.2 billion) on Thursday.

Toyota's results were boosted by weakness in the Japanese yen as well as strong hybrid vehicle demand in the U.S. However, the increase in operating income was its first in six quarters.

Broadly, the changes to earnings and outlooks come as production for the global industry slows.

Consulting and insights firm GlobalData expects global light-vehicle production of about 90.96 million units in 2026, down 2.1% compared with last year. It forecast a production increase of less than 1% next year. That comes on the heels of strong annual growth earlier this decade, led by China.

Cox Automotive reported the average transaction price of a new U.S. vehicle in September was more than $50,500. That was just shy of the record of $50,614 in December 2025.

Lofty vehicle prices have led to record-high and record-long financing deals, as well as concerns that customers are getting priced out of the new-vehicle market.

The typical U.S. new-vehicle payment reached $776 a month in September, the highest since December 2023, according to Cox Automotive.

Cox Automotive chief economist Jeremy Robb, discussing the third quarter for the automotive industry, rated the overall economy, buyer ability and borrowing costs as cautionary "yellow lights."

But he did have some "green lights," such as good credit availability and employment conditions, which could give some relief for automakers and consumers, many of whom need vehicles for their everyday lives.

Robb said there's a "tug-of-war" between headwinds such as rising costs, interest rates and fuel prices and tailwinds such as growth in liquid assets and savings that has helped offset some of the additional costs.

"Consumers remain under financial pressure, but the vehicle demand continues to hold, showing more resiliency in the auto industry than we've seen in other parts of the economy," Robb said during a Sept. 24 call, noting consumer sentiment remains low.

#755. Ancient Siberian tomb reveals surprising secrets of cannabis use 2,800 years ago

A remarkable discovery in a nearly 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb has provided the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence that people used cannabis for its intoxicating effects. By examining ancient cannabis seeds and chemical traces preserved in human hair, researchers have uncovered new clues about the role of the plant in prehistoric burial rituals.

Cannabis is among the most widely used psychoactive plants in the modern world, but tracing its use thousands of years into the past presents a major archaeological challenge. Flowers, leaves, and resins tend to decompose over time, leaving little physical evidence behind. Ancient communities also relied on cannabis for practical purposes, including producing fiber and oil, making it difficult to distinguish these uses from medicinal or recreational consumption.

An international team led by Dr. Gino Caspari, affiliated with the Institute of Archaeological Sciences at the University of Bern and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, investigated an elaborate tomb in the Republic of Tyva in southern Siberia. The burial site belonged to prominent members of the Scythians, a culture known for its skilled horseback riders who inhabited the vast Eurasian steppe.

Ancient Siberian Tomb Contains 1,000 Cannabis Seeds

During the investigation, researchers recovered approximately 1,000 cannabis seeds from the tomb. They used radiocarbon dating to determine the age of six individual seeds. Combined with other dating evidence, the results indicate that the seeds were deposited in the burial site during the early eighth century B.C.

"The seeds show that cannabis played an important role in the rituals surrounding the burial," says Caspari, an archaeologist and the study's lead author.

The researchers also analyzed human hair preserved in the tomb's central burial chamber. Chemical evidence in several samples pointed to cannabis consumption, providing a crucial connection between the plant remains and the people buried at the site.

"This study is particularly insightful because it combines the analysis of plant remains with molecular traces in the human body," says Caspari.

The findings were published in the journal Science.

Chemical Traces in Ancient Hair Reveal Cannabis Use

Although the cannabis seeds were remarkably well preserved, their presence alone could not establish whether the plant was used for its mind-altering effects. The seeds probably came from wild cannabis plants, and researchers could not determine whether people had deliberately cultivated them for their psychoactive properties.

The strongest evidence came from the preserved human hair. Using high-resolution mass spectrometry and other analytical techniques, the team identified clear chemical signals consistent with cannabinol (CBN) in several samples.

CBN can form when tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary compound responsible for cannabis intoxication, undergoes oxidation. The researchers also detected weaker signals that matched the mass of THC, further supporting the possibility that the individuals had consumed cannabis.

While these chemical findings indicate cannabis use, they cannot reveal how much was consumed or exactly how the compounds entered the body. The individuals may have inhaled cannabis smoke or consumed the plant in another way, but the available evidence cannot establish a particular method.

Other archaeological discoveries from later periods in Central Asia provide clearer evidence of cannabis inhalation. At those sites, researchers have identified cannabinoid residues on heated stones and inside vessels, pointing to the use of heat to release compounds that could be inhaled.

"The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties," says Caspari, who conducts research at the Institute of Archaeological Sciences at the University of Bern and the Max Planck Institute for Geoanthropology in Jena (Germany).

Cannabis, Horse Sacrifices, and Ancient Burial Rituals

The cannabis evidence was discovered within an elaborate ceremonial burial site, suggesting that the plant may have been connected to important Scythian funerary traditions.

"In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well," says Gino Caspari.

Earlier research at the site identified the remains of 18 horses that had been deliberately positioned on the burial mound. Continued excavations have since uncovered evidence of several dozen more sacrificed horses, along with scattered human bones.

These discoveries reveal the extraordinary scale of the burial ceremonies and provide important context for understanding why cannabis may have been included among the materials deposited in the tomb.

Oldest Directly Dated Evidence of Cannabis Intoxication

Taken together, the seeds and chemical traces in human hair represent the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence currently known for cannabis use associated with intoxication.

However, several questions remain unanswered. The researchers cannot determine how much THC the ancient cannabis contained, whether the plants were particularly potent, or whether Scythian communities had begun deliberately selecting or cultivating cannabis varieties with higher concentrations of psychoactive compounds.

To investigate these questions, the team is now studying genetic material recovered from the ancient plant remains. The unusually good preservation of the cannabis DNA could provide valuable insights into how humans domesticated the plant and how it spread across different regions over thousands of years.

"We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples," says Gino Caspari. "DNA preservation is excellent in this case. This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of this crop soon."

Materials provided by University of Bern. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

The adjusted figure is a non-GAAP measure, meaning it leaves out certain items counted under generally accepted accounting principles, or GAAP, the standard U.S. accounting rules. Overseas membership revenue grew nearly 30% year over year. On iQIYI International, the C-drama “Overdo” topped the rankings in 34 countries and regions during its first week and held the top C-drama position on Google Trends during peak viewing. The Indonesian original drama “Dangerous Rose” also took the top spot in Indonesia during its opening week on the service. Overseas microdramas also grew, the company said. In Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia, iQIYI widened its bundled memberships offered through local telecom operators.

Gong said: “Our shift towards becoming a long-form video social media, with long-form video at the core and decentralization and AI as twin engines, is yielding encouraging initial results.”
